rounds.text: United Drilling Tools Ltd trades at a modest price-to-book ratio of 1.67x against a book value of ₹ 138 per share, sitting favourably below the sector benchmark price-to-book ratio of 2.42x [E2, E7]. Furthermore, the company delivers a return on assets of 6.6%, which edges out the sector benchmark of 6.29% [E8]. From a valuation perspective, a discounted cash flow analysis calculates an intrinsic value of ₹ 401 per share compared to the current market price of ₹ 230, providing a substantial margin of safety of 42.7% [E41, E42]. Adding to this undervaluation signal, a reverse discounted cash flow indicates that the prevailing market price only prices in an earnings growth rate of 10.3%, whereas the base case anticipates an 18.0% growth rate [E43]. Conceded: the company registers a low median return on equity of 6% over the last 3 years and 8% over 5 years, accompanied by a modest dividend yield of 0.78% [E4, E22, E23].

United Drilling Tools Ltd currently trades at a P/E ratio of 22.9x, which is essentially identical to the sector benchmark of 22.89x [E1, E6]. This valuation is difficult to justify given the company’s persistent underperformance in capital efficiency, evidenced by a Return on Equity (ROE) that has stagnated at 7% [E13, E64]. The long-term trend is even more concerning, as the median ROE has declined from 8% over the last five years to just 6% over the last three years [E22, E23]. This downward trajectory in profitability is further highlighted by the company’s low three-year average ROE of 5.55% [E58]. Conceded: the company maintains a P/B ratio of 1.66x against a sector benchmark of 2.42x, and a DCF model suggests an intrinsic value of Rs 401 per share [E7, E41]. Despite these metrics, the market is currently pricing in an earnings growth rate of 10.3%, which appears aggressive for a business struggling to generate meaningful returns on its equity [E23, E43].

Conceded: the company's median return on equity is 8% over 5 years and 6% over 3 years [E22, E23], and its ROE sits at 7% [E13]. However, dismissing the valuation because of these ROE figures ignores a critical asset-efficiency metric: the company's Return on Assets (ROA) of 6.6% actually outperforms the sector benchmark of 6.29% [E8]. Furthermore, the bear's claim that the implied earnings growth rate of 10.3% is too aggressive [E43] misses the fundamental undervaluation shown by the discounted cash flow model, which places intrinsic value at a substantial premium and provides a wide margin of safety of 42.7% [E41, E42]. Finally, while the P/E ratio aligns with the sector [E1, E6], the Price-to-Book ratio of 1.66x trades at a sharp discount to the sector benchmark of 2.42x [E7], proving that the market is under-appreciating the underlying asset value relative to peers.

The bull’s reliance on ROA [E8] to excuse poor profitability is misleading because it ignores the consistent, multi-year trend of declining returns on equity [E22, E23, E24]. While the bull highlights a 6.6% ROA [E8], this metric is overshadowed by the company’s actual ROE of 7% [E13, E64], which significantly underperforms the sector benchmark of 10.77% [E9]. Conceded: the P/B ratio of 1.66x is lower than the sector benchmark of 2.42x [E7]. However, this discount is justified by the company’s inability to generate competitive returns, as evidenced by the 3-year median ROE of only 6% [E23] and the recent flag for low ROE [E58]. The bull’s reliance on a DCF model [E41, E42] is speculative, as it assumes an aggressive 18% growth rate that contradicts the company's historical performance [E43]. Furthermore, the market price is already trading at 67% of its 52-week range [E5], suggesting that the "undervaluation" cited by the bull is not shared by the broader market.
